description_full: BOK Financial Corporation operates as the financial holding company for BOKF, NA that provides various financial products and services in Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Northwest Arkansas, Colorado, Arizona, and Kansas/Missouri. It operates through three segments: Commercial Banking, Consumer Banking, and Wealth Management. The Commercial Banking segment offers lending, treasury, cash management, and customer commodity risk management products for small businesses, middle market, and larger commercial customers, as well as operates TransFund electronic funds transfer network. The Consumer Banking segment engages in the provision of retail lending and deposit services to small business customers through retail branch network; and mortgage loan origination and servicing activities. The Wealth Management segment offers fiduciary, private bank, insurance, and investment advisory services; and brokerage and trading services primarily related to providing liquidity to the mortgage markets through trading of U.S. government agency mortgage-backed securities and related derivative contracts, as well as underwrites state and municipal securities. The company also provides commercial loans, such as loans for working capital, facilities acquisition or expansion, purchases of equipment, and other needs of commercial customers; and service, healthcare, energy, and other sector loans. In addition, it offers commercial real estate loans for the construction of buildings or other improvements to real estate and property held by borrowers for investment purposes; residential mortgage and personal loans; and personal and small business checking, online bill paying, mobile banking, automated teller machine, and call centers services. The company was founded in 1910 and is headquartered in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

financial_summary: BOK Financial Corporation is a mid-cap financial services business with a $7.9B market cap on $2.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $575M in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.28× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.4× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 7.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 63% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 34% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.31x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 514 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 20% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.24 vs 5y 0.82), so read it loosely.
About $30.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash, 37% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $77.84 (margin of safety -67%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $52.90 to $112 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 34% above its 10-year median.
The 9 covering analysts target $143 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 10.1% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.59).
It converts 26% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 2.92% and an efficiency ratio of 62%.
It earns a 10% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 12.3% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.54% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.5% over 3 years, 2.2% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 9% of profits supports about 0.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 12.3% on average.
Analysts expect 2.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 63.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 36%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $2.0M sold).
It returns 7.1% a year to shareholders (5.2% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years.
Short interest is elevated at 12.9% of the float, 10.7 days to cover.
people: With about 4,982 employees, each generates about $437K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and revenue has grown 3.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $115K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.0M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
